title: The routine of a Gursikh
hook: Guru Ram Das's salok on the Guru's Sikh: up early, bathed, remembering the Name (Gauri Var M4, ang 305)

segments.voice: Yesterday we closed Guru Amar Das: humility, equality, and a kitchen where anyone could sit and eat. Your line was open kitchen. Did a door of yours open, even a little? Day one thousand one hundred ninety-two.

Whoever calls himself a Sikh of the Guru. That's how a short salok begins, in Guru Ram Das's ballad in Raga Gauri. Notice the opening. Not whoever was born into a Sikh family. Not whoever knows the hymns by heart. Whoever claims the name. And then, instead of a definition, the salok hands you a clock. It walks through what that claim looks like before the sun is up. Today a new voice on the path: Guru Ram Das, whose hymns carry the heading Mahala four. And the first thing we hear from him is a morning.
screen: `WHOEVER CALLS HIMSELF A SIKH.` → `NOT A DEFINITION, A CLOCK.` → `MAHALA FOUR.`

segments.voice: Here's the first half of the salok, paraphrased. The one who calls himself a Sikh of the Guru rises in the early hours and dwells on the Lord's Name. He makes the effort, early in the morning, bathes, and dips in the pool of nectar. Following the Guru's teaching, he repeats the Name, and his faults and wrongs fall away. Three things stand out. First, a name turns into a habit. The salok doesn't argue about who counts as a Sikh. It describes a morning and lets the morning answer. Second, the word for effort, udam. Rising early isn't treated as a personality type, the lucky few who wake up cheerful. It's something you make the effort to do, the same way a farmer gets up to water a field. Third, the pool of nectar. Some readers hear a real bath, the body washed before the day. Others hear the pool as the Name itself, where the mind gets washed. Some teachers hold both together: wash the body, then let the Name wash the rest. Sikhs call those early hours amrit vela, the ambrosial time, a phrase from Guru Nanak's Japji. One more piece sits just outside the salok: the sangat. The salok itself doesn't name it, but for Sikhs near a gurdwara, the morning can mean walking in to hear the prayers with others. So the routine of a Gursikh isn't a rulebook. It's a picture of a person whose day starts with remembering, on purpose, before anything else gets a vote.
screen: `A NAME TURNS INTO A HABIT.` · `UDAM: THE EFFORT TO RISE.` · `THE POOL OF NECTAR, BODY AND MIND.` · `BEFORE ANYTHING ELSE GETS A VOTE.` · then, large: `THE ROUTINE OF A GURSIKH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: plan to rise earlier, once. In the sit, settle the breath and picture tomorrow's first minutes. Choose a time a little earlier than usual, not heroic, just a little. Then choose what the first thing will be: washing your face slowly, a line of Gurbani, a few quiet breaths before the phone. Hold that picture until it feels doable. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
The routine of a Gursikh. Guru Ram Das's salok: rise early, make the effort, bathe, and dwell on the Name before the day begins. Today's word.
screen: `THE ROUTINE OF A GURSIKH — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the gursikh's morning. Tonight, set the alarm a little earlier, and put one thing beside the bed that you want to meet first. Day one thousand one hundred ninety-two.

howItsDone: Sikhs who keep the daily discipline rise in the early hours, bathe, and recite the morning prayers, beginning with the Japji; this salok of Guru Ram Das is one of the passages Sikh teachers turn to when they describe the Sikh day.
